subsection: 6. Direct Rule and the search for a settlement, 1974–1993

notes.h: Direct Rule and its secretaries of state, 1974–1993
notes.b: Direct Rule was run from London for almost twenty years, through a succession of Secretaries of State who tried and failed to restore devolved government.
points: Direct Rule continued after the collapse of Sunningdale in 1974, with the Secretary of State and the Northern Ireland Office responsible for government.

The Secretaries of State included Merlyn Rees (1974 to 1976), Roy Mason (1976 to 1979), Humphrey Atkins (1979 to 1981), Jim Prior (1981 to 1984), Douglas Hurd (1984 to 1985), Tom King (1985 to 1989), Peter Brooke (1989 to 1992) and Patrick Mayhew (1992 to 1997).
The Constitutional Convention of 1975 to 1976 was elected to find a devolved settlement, but its proposals for power sharing were rejected and it collapsed in March 1976.
Under 'Ulsterisation' from 1976, the security role of the British army was reduced in favour of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
The policy of criminalisation ended special category status for prisoners convicted of terrorist offences from 1 March 1976.
British governments ruled out a return to the unionist majority rule that had ended in 1972, so any future government had to be shared between the communities.

notes.b: The Peace People movement began after three children were killed in Belfast in August 1976, and it brought thousands of women onto the streets.
points: On 10 August 1976 three children were killed in Belfast when a car, whose driver had been shot by a British soldier, crashed into them.
Betty Williams, a Belfast woman who witnessed the crash, and Mairead Corrigan, the children's aunt, led the first peace march.
The movement organised large peace rallies in Belfast and across Northern Ireland, and it appealed to both communities to end the violence.
The Peace People were a participant movement of ordinary people, and they called for an end to paramilitary violence on all sides.
Williams and Corrigan were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1976, which was announced in 1977.
Contemporaries praised the movement but some republicans and loyalists dismissed it as naive, while historians see it as a significant expression of popular peace feeling.

notes.h: The H-Blocks, the blanket protest and the hunger strikes, 1976–1981
notes.b: The prison protests over political status at the Maze prison, known as the H-Blocks, led to the 1981 hunger strikes, which made Bobby Sands a symbol across Ireland.
points: After special category status ended on 1 March 1976, republican prisoners refused to wear prison uniform and began the blanket protest.
The protest escalated into the dirty protest from 1978, when prisoners refused to wash or leave their cells.
Bobby Sands began a hunger strike on 1 March 1981 to demand the restoration of political status, and he died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days.
Sands was elected MP for Fermanagh and South Tyrone in April 1981, while he was on hunger strike, and his election gave the protest wide publicity.
Nine further hunger strikers died between May and August 1981, and the total number of deaths in the hunger strike was ten.
The hunger strike ended in October 1981 without the British government granting political status, although some concessions were made on prison conditions.

notes.b: Sinn Féin moved from abstentionist politics towards electoral contests after the hunger strikes, arguing that the republican struggle could be fought at the ballot box as well as by violence.
points: Sinn Féin decided in the early 1980s to contest elections, and its strategy is summed up in the phrase 'the armalite and the ballot box', associated with Danny Morrison in 1981.
Owen Carron won the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election in August 1981 after Sands died, and he took the seat as a Sinn Féin candidate.
Sinn Féin candidates won seats in the 1982 Northern Ireland Assembly election, and Gerry Adams was among those elected.
In 1983 Gerry Adams won the West Belfast seat at Westminster, defeating Gerry Fitt, and Sinn Féin members who were elected refused to take their seats in Westminster.
The strategy was a deliberate move to build political support, and critics saw it as a cover for continued IRA violence.

notes.b: Adams was the Sinn Féin leader who turned the party into an electoral force, and he became the main republican interlocutor with the British and Irish governments.
points: Gerry Adams was born in 1948 in Belfast and grew up in a republican family in West Belfast.
He was interned in 1971 and became a prominent Sinn Féin member in the 1970s and 1980s.
He was elected president of Sinn Féin in 1983, a post he held for decades, and he led the party's move into electoral politics.
He was a participant in the republican movement's negotiations with the SDLP's John Hume from 1988.
Contemporaries saw him as the political face of the IRA, and in 1988 the Home Secretary banned broadcasts of the voices of Sinn Féin spokespeople, including Adams.
Historians differ on his role, with some seeing him as the architect of Sinn Féin's shift to politics and others arguing that the shift was a tactical change within a continuing campaign.

notes.h: The New Ireland Forum and Thatcher's response, 1983–1984
notes.b: The New Ireland Forum brought together the constitutional nationalist parties of Ireland, and its three options were rejected by the British Prime Minister.
points: The Forum was set up in 1983 by the Dublin government, and it included the SDLP, Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and the Labour Party, while Sinn Féin was excluded.
The unionist parties boycotted the Forum, which meant that its report reflected the views of the nationalist parties and the Dublin government.
The Forum's report, published in May 1984, set out three options: a unitary Irish state, a confederal arrangement, and joint authority between Britain and Ireland.
Margaret Thatcher rejected all three options at a press conference in November 1984, saying 'Out, out, out' in response to the proposals.
Thatcher's rejection of the Forum's options marked the limits of British willingness to change Northern Ireland's constitutional position in the mid-1980s.

notes.h: The Brighton bombing and the Hume–Adams dialogue
notes.b: The IRA bomb at Brighton in October 1984 was an attempt to kill the British government, and the secret dialogue between Hume and Adams from 1988 explored a route to peace.
points: On 12 October 1984 the IRA bombed the Grand Hotel in Brighton, where the Conservative Party conference was being held.
Five people were killed in the bombing, but Margaret Thatcher and most of her cabinet escaped.
The Hume–Adams dialogue began in 1988 as a secret exchange of views between the SDLP leader and the Sinn Féin president.
The talks were controversial, with unionists and some nationalists objecting to any contact between the SDLP and Sinn Féin while the IRA campaign continued.
The dialogue was an early attempt to find common ground between constitutional nationalism and republicanism, and it is seen by historians as a precursor to later peace efforts.

notes.b: Thatcher was the British Prime Minister who led the government through the hunger strikes and signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement, a shift in British policy.
points: Margaret Thatcher was Prime Minister from May 1979 to November 1990, and she made security and the defeat of terrorism central to her policy in Northern Ireland.
She refused to grant political status to the hunger strikers, and her government held firm during the 1981 protest.
She signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with the Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald at Hillsborough Castle on 15 November 1985, giving the Irish government a formal consultative role.
She was a participant in the negotiations and the decision to sign the Agreement, which she took despite strong opposition from unionists.
Contemporary unionists regarded her as having betrayed the Union, while nationalists welcomed the Agreement as a sign of British recognition of an Irish interest.
Historians differ on her motives, with some stressing security cooperation with Dublin and others seeing the Agreement as a pragmatic response to the failure of other approaches.

notes.b: Molyneaux led the Ulster Unionist Party through the period of the Anglo-Irish Agreement and was the main voice of mainstream unionist opposition.
points: James Molyneaux was born in 1920 and was MP for South Antrim from 1970, and he became leader of the Ulster Unionist Party in 1979.
He led the unionist opposition to the Anglo-Irish Agreement, and he worked with Ian Paisley on the 'Ulster says No' campaign.
He was a participant in the unionist campaign of 1985 and 1986, which included protests, a rally in Belfast and the resignation of unionist MPs from Westminster.
Contemporaries valued his caution and his commitment to the Union, although some unionists felt he was too passive in opposing the Agreement.
Historians regard him as a steady leader of mainstream unionism who opposed the Agreement without the confrontational style of Paisley.

notes.h: Key personality: John Hume (part 3, SDLP leader and the Hume–Adams talks)
notes.b: Hume led the SDLP from 1979 and became the leading constitutional nationalist voice, with his dialogue with Sinn Féin reshaping the search for peace.
points: John Hume was leader of the SDLP from 1979, and he was elected to the European Parliament in 1979.
He supported the Anglo-Irish Agreement, arguing that it gave nationalists a role in Northern Ireland's government.
He began the dialogue with Gerry Adams in 1988, and he argued that the IRA campaign must end before republicans could take part in politics.
He was a participant in the Brooke-Mayhew talks, which tried to set up a new devolved settlement in 1991 and 1992.
Contemporaries saw him as a moderate and effective nationalist leader, while unionists criticised him for talking to Sinn Féin.
Historians credit him with shaping the nationalist case for a peace process based on consent and dialogue, and his approach influenced the Downing Street Declaration.

notes.b: The Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Republic a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland, and it was the biggest British policy shift since Sunningdale.
points: The Agreement was signed on 15 November 1985 at Hillsborough Castle by Margaret Thatcher and Garret FitzGerald.
It set up an Intergovernmental Conference, with a permanent secretariat at Maryfield near Belfast, through which the Irish government could put forward views on Northern Ireland.
The Agreement affirmed that there would be no change in the status of Northern Ireland without the consent of its majority, while accepting that the Irish government had an interest in its affairs.
Unionists responded with the slogan 'Ulster says No' and with mass protests across Northern Ireland in the weeks after the signing.
Unionist MPs resigned their Westminster seats in January 1986 to force by-elections, but the Agreement remained in force.
Republicans rejected the Agreement because it did not end British jurisdiction, and it was seen by nationalists as a limited but real step towards Irish involvement.

notes.h: The Brooke-Mayhew talks and the Downing Street Declaration
notes.b: The talks of 1991 and 1992 failed to produce a settlement, and the Downing Street Declaration of 1993 set out the principles on which later peace efforts were built.
points: Peter Brooke, as Secretary of State, said in 1990 that Britain had no selfish strategic or economic interest in Northern Ireland.
The Brooke initiative of 1991 and the Mayhew talks of 1992 brought the parties together in multi-party talks, but they did not produce agreement.
The Downing Street Declaration was issued on 15 December 1993 by Prime Minister John Major and Taoiseach Albert Reynolds.
The declaration recognised the right of the Irish people as a whole to self-determination, and it said that a united Ireland would require the consent of a majority in Northern Ireland.
It set out the British government's acceptance that it would not stand in the way of a united Ireland if a majority wished it, and it invited republicans to renounce violence.

notes.h: Assessment: the search for a settlement, 1974–1993
points: Achievement: the Anglo-Irish Agreement gave the Irish government a formal consultative role in Northern Ireland's affairs, the most significant such role since Sunningdale.
Achievement: the Downing Street Declaration set out principles of consent and self-determination that became the basis for later agreements.
Limit: between 1974 and 1993 no devolved government was restored, and Direct Rule remained the basis of British policy.
Limit: the Hume-Adams dialogue and the Brooke and Mayhew talks did not end the IRA campaign, and violence continued throughout the period.
Contemporary view: nationalists and the Irish government saw the Anglo-Irish Agreement and the Declaration as steps towards justice and peace.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the Agreement as an infringement of their constitutional rights, and they resisted the Declaration's principles of joint authority.
Later view: historians see the period as one in which the framework for peace was built gradually, through dialogue, agreements and the acceptance of consent as a principle.

keyTerms.definition: The government of Northern Ireland from Westminster through a Secretary of State, which continued from 1972 until devolution was restored later, and which dominated policy between 1974 and 1993.
The use of violence against civilians and the state for political ends, which the British government sought to defeat through security policy and political negotiation.
A system of government in which unionists and nationalists share power, which British governments sought but failed to restore between 1974 and 1993.
Materials and messages used to shape public opinion, which the British government and republicans both used during the hunger strikes and the Anglo-Irish negotiations.
The 1985 agreement between Thatcher and FitzGerald that gave the Irish government a consultative role in Northern Ireland through an Intergovernmental Conference.
The 15 December 1993 declaration by Major and Reynolds that accepted the principle of self-determination and majority consent for any change in Northern Ireland's status.
The policy from 1976 of transferring the security role of the British army to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
A refusal of food by prisoners to press for political status, which in 1981 led to ten deaths including Bobby Sands.

Sands began his hunger strike on 1 March 1981 and died on 5 May 1981 after 66 days.

Owen Carron won the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election in August 1981 after the death of Bobby Sands.
